'''Bradley Cardinale''' is an American ecologist, conservation biologist, academic and researcher. He is currently a professor in the Department of Ecosystem Science and Management at Penn State University.

Cardinale's work has focused on the conservation and restoration of [[biodiversity]] in natural systems, as well as the [[ecological design]] of human engineered systems that benefit from biodiversity.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_videos.jsp?cntn_id=118945&media_id=69371&org=NSF|title=Bradley Cardinale of the University of Michigan discusses how biodiversity promotes water quality}}</ref> He uses mathematical models, lab- and field-based experiments, observational studies of natural ecosystems, and meta-analyses of existing data to examine how human activities impact Earth's biological diversity, and to protect and manage species, their [[ecosystem]]s, and the services they provide to society. He has written over 150 scientific papers, as well as a textbook on [[conservation biology]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=6603742749|title=Bradley Cardinale - Scopus}}</ref>

Cardinale is an elected fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lsa.umich.edu/eeb/news-events/all-news/archived-news/2013/12/cardinale-named-aaas-fellow.html|title=Bradley Cardinale}}</ref> and the [[Ecological Society of America]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esa.org/programs/fellows-program/esa-fellows/#esatoggle-shortcode-content-72|title=ESA Fellows}}</ref> In 2014, Cardinale was named by [[Thomson Reuters]] as one of The World's Most Influential Scientific Minds.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://homes.esat.kuleuven.be/~bdmdotbe/bdm2013/documents/worlds-most-influential-scientific-minds-2014.pdf|title=The World's Most Influential Scientific Minds 2014}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Cardinale was born in [[Phoenix, Arizona]] in 1969. He studied at [[Arizona State University]] where, in 1993, he received a B.S. in biology.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://seas.umich.edu/research/faculty/brad_cardinale|title=Bradley J. Cardinale}}</ref>

After receiving his bachelor's degree, Cardinale went on to receive an M.S. in Fisheries and Wildlife in 1996 from [[Michigan State University]] where he helped develop methods for restoring coastal wetlands in the [[Great Lakes]]. He then went on to complete a Ph.D. in biology from the [[University of Maryland]] in 2002 where he led projects focused on the restoration of biodiversity and ecosystem processes in degraded streams in the [[Appalachian Mountains]]. Following his Ph.D., Cardinale completed a postdoctoral fellowship in the Department of Zoology at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ciglr.seas.umich.edu/people/bradley-j-cardinale/|title=Bradley J. Cardinale}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 2005, Cardinale joined the Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Marine Biology at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] as an assistant professor, becoming associate professor in 2010. In 2011, he left the University of California, Santa Barbara to join the [[University of Michigan]], where he became a full professor in 2015. He served as coordinator of the Conservation Ecology Program at the University of Michigan from 2012 to 2014.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://research.ku.edu/sites/research.ku.edu/files/docs/searches/bradley-cardinale-cv-web.pdf|title=Bradley Cardinale - CV}}</ref> He left the University of Michigan in 2021 to join Penn State University as head of the Department of Ecosystem Science and Management.<ref name=PSU>{{cite web|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/642600/2020/12/16/academics/bradley-j-cardinale-named-head-department-ecosystem-science|title=Bradley J. Cardinale named head of Department of Ecosystem Science & Management}}</ref>

In 2013, he was elected by the U.S. National Academy of Science as one of three U.S. representatives on the inaugural Science Committee of the [[United Nations]] initiative [[Future Earth]]. Future Earth was a reorganization of the [[United Nations Environmental Programme]] (UNEP) that merged five discipline-based global change programs into a single, multidisciplinary research program.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://futureearth.org/2014/07/01/members-of-future-earth-science-committee-listed-among-the-worlds-most-influential-scientific-minds-2014/|title=Members of Future Earth Science Committee listed among 'The World's Most Influential Scientific Minds 2014'}}</ref>

Between 2009 and 2013, Cardinale helped form the U.S. [[National Ecological Observatory Network]] (NEON), assisting with selection of the core aquatic sites, and serving on the Pacific-Southwest Domain Science Committee. He was also co-PI with Walter Dodds and [[Margaret A. Palmer]] on the proposal that established the Stream Observational and Experimental Network (STREON) – a coordinated set of national [[climate change]] experiments that were ultimately eliminated from NEON as part of budget cuts and descoping.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Long-term Experimental Networks for Stream Ecosystem Studies: the Lotic Intersite Nitrogen Experiment (LINX) and the Stream Experimental and Observatory Network (STREON) Component of the National Ecological Observatory Network|bibcode = 2008AGUFM.H12A..01M|last1 = Mulholland|first1 = P. J.|last2 = Dodds|first2 = W. K.|last3 = Palmer|first3 = M. A.|last4 = Cardinale|first4 = B. J.|journal = AGU Fall Meeting Abstracts|volume = 2008|pages = H12A–01|year = 2008}}</ref>

Cardinale received the Hynes Award for New Investigators from the [[Society for Freshwater Science]] in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://freshwater-science.org/awards-programs/hynes-award|title=Hynes Award}}</ref> He also received the [[Burton V. Barnes]] Award from the [[Sierra Club]] in 2015 for his leadership in organizing academic scientists at 13 state-universities in Michigan to speak out against anti-biodiversity legislation that was intended to make state lands more accessible to fracking, lumbering, and mining. That effort ultimately led to the legislation being vetoed by Michigan's governor.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cardinale.seas.umich.edu/portfolio/cardinale-receives-the-burton-v-barnes-award-from-mi-sierra-club/|title=Cardinale receives the Burton V. Barnes Award, MI Sierra Club}}</ref>

In 2016, Cardinale was appointed as the director of Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research (CIGLR). CIGLR is one of 16 Cooperative Institutes across the U.S. that are funded by NOAA to link government research labs to university partners, non-governmental organizations, and private business partners who help them accomplish their research and development goals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cardinale.seas.umich.edu/portfolio/u-m-wins-cooperative-institute-for-great-lakes-research/|title=U-M wins Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research}}</ref>

== Research and work ==
Cardinale's research focuses on the conservation and restoration of biodiversity, as well as the use of ecological design to improve human engineered ecosystems. Most of his work has focused on the management of biodiversity in freshwater habitats (streams, lakes, wetlands), though he has worked in ecosystems as diverse as grasslands, forests, and kelp beds.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=N9f43xoAAAAJ&hl=en|title=Bradley Cardinale - Google Scholar}}</ref>

Work from the Cardinale Lab has received extensive recognition in the popular media, leading to numerous interviews on U.S. National Public Radio (NPR),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.news.ucsb.edu/2009/012642/ecology-evolution-and-marine-biology-scholar-receives-harold-j-plous-award|title=Ecology, Evolution, and Marine Biology Scholar Receives Harold J. Plous Award|date=16 June 2009 }}</ref> and coverage in Reuters,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-biodiversity-streams-idUSTRE7355ML20110406|title=Biodiversity vital to streams as extinctions rise|newspaper=Reuters |date=6 April 2011 }}</ref> the British Broadcast Corporation (BBC),<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/3707857.stm|title=Conservation 'needs wider view'|date=13 May 2004 }}</ref> and the Canadian Broadcast Corporation (CBC).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/technology/technology-blog/2007/11/extinctions-could-cut-plant-productivity-in-half.html|title=Extinctions could cut plant productivity in half}}</ref>

=== Conservation biology ===
A significant part of Cardinale's research has focused on developing a key argument for biodiversity conservation, which is that biodiversity is the foundation for a healthy planet. His work has shown that [[loss of biodiversity]] impacts important ecological processes that are essential to the productivity and stability of ecosystems, as well as the goods and services they provide to humans.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225283251|title=Biodiversity loss and its impact on humanity}}</ref>

Cardinale and his colleagues have developed a suite of mathematical models to describe how the biological traits of species, interactions among species, and the structure of entire food webs influence essential processes like primary production, decomposition, and nutrient cycling.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Food-web interactions govern the resistance of communities after non-random extinctions|pmid = 15141210|year = 2004|last1 = Ives|first1 = A. R.|last2 = Cardinale|first2 = B. J.|journal = Nature|volume = 429|issue = 6988|pages = 174–7|doi = 10.1038/nature02515|bibcode = 2004Natur.429..174I|s2cid = 4351240}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Effects of species diversity on the primary productivity of ecosystems: extending our spatial and temporal scales of inference|doi=10.1111/j.0030-1299.2004.13254.x|year=2004|last1=Cardinale|first1=Bradley J.|last2=Ives|first2=Anthony R.|last3=Inchausti|first3=Pablo|journal=Oikos|volume=104|issue=3|pages=437–450|bibcode=2004Oikos.104..437C }}</ref> He has tested the predictions of these models in both field and lab-based experiments, primarily using freshwater organisms as model systems. His experiments were among the first to show that biodiversity enhances the efficiency and productivity of ecosystems through niche partitioning among species,<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/news/2011/110406/full/news.2011.216.html|title=Algae biodiversity cleans streams|year=2011 |doi=10.1038/news.2011.216 |last1=Gewin |first1=Virginia |journal=Nature |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and via facilitative interactions that cause diverse communities to be greater than the sum-of-their-parts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2002/01/020130074549.htm|title=Research Shows Why More Species Are Better For Ecosystems
}}</ref> These mechanisms had long-been presumed to operate in nature, but empirical evidence was lacking.

Cardinale is perhaps best known for his leadership in organizing major data syntheses that have helped foster a consensus about the probable consequences of biodiversity loss for humanity. He has organized numerous working groups funded by the U.S. [[National Science Foundation]], the United Nations Environmental Program, the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, and the Socio-Economic Environmental Synthesis Center.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/featured/cardinale|title=Biodiversity and the Functioning of Ecosystems: Translating Results from Model Experiments into Functional Reality}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.sesync.org/linking-biodiversity-and-ecosystem-services|title= Linking Biodiversity & Ecosystem Services: From Expert Opinion to Prediction & Application|newspaper= Sesync|date= 18 January 2013}}</ref> In these working groups, Cardinale and his colleagues have assembled extensive datasets of thousands of experiments<ref>{{cite journal|title=Effects of biodiversity on the functioning of ecosystems: a summary of 164 experimental manipulations of species richness|doi=10.1890/08-1584.1|year=2009|last1=Cardinale|first1=Bradley J.|last2=Srivastava|first2=Diane S.|last3=Duffy|first3=J. Emmett|last4=Wright|first4=Justin P.|last5=Downing|first5=Amy L.|last6=Sankaran|first6=Mahesh|last7=Jouseau|first7=Claire|last8=Cadotte|first8=Marc W.|last9=Carroll|first9=Ian T.|last10=Weis|first10=Jerome J.|last11=Hector|first11=Andy|last12=Loreau|first12=Michel|journal=Ecology|volume=90|issue=3|page=854|doi-access=free|bibcode=2009Ecol...90..854C }}</ref> and observational studies<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature23886|title=Biodiversity effects in the wild are common and as strong as key drivers of productivit|year=2017 |doi=10.1038/nature23886 |last1=Duffy |first1=J. Emmett |last2=Godwin |first2=Casey M. |last3=Cardinale |first3=Bradley J. |journal=Nature |volume=549 |issue=7671 |pages=261–264 |pmid=28869964 |bibcode=2017Natur.549..261D |s2cid=4459856 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/09/170911122625.htm|title=Biodiversity just as powerful as climate change for healthy ecosystems}}</ref> that have quantified how changes in biodiversity impact a wide variety of ecological processes and [[ecosystem service]]s for organisms inhabiting 30 biomes on 5 continents. Their syntheses have led to publication of 15 formal meta-analyses.

In 2012, Cardinale organized and led an invited review for a special issue of Nature dedicated to the 20th anniversary of the Rio Earth Summit in which his colleagues and he synthesized over 1,700 papers that have examined biodiversity's impact on 34 ecosystem goods and services. This synthesis revealed a remarkable level of generality in how biodiversity impacts the functioning of Earth's ecosystems and the services they provide to society.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.umich.edu/20-years-after-rio-earth-summit-ecologists-call-for-preservation-of-planet-s-remaining-biological-diversity/|title=20 years after Rio Earth Summit: Ecologists call for preservation of planet's remaining biological diversity|date=6 June 2012 }}</ref> Recently, Cardinale and colleagues have extended the idea of ecosystem services to the realm of national security, showing how nature mitigates conflicts and disasters that lead to security crises.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Nature's role in national security|doi=10.1016/j.nbsj.2026.100330|year=2026|last1=Cardinale|first1=B.J.|last2=Duffy|first2=J.E.|last3=Schoonover|first3=R.|journal=Nature-Based Solutions|volume=9|issue=1 |article-number=100330}}</ref>

=== Restoration ecology ===
Cardinale has also conducted considerable research on the restoration of ecosystems and their biodiversity. During his early graduate studies, Cardinale worked on restoration of Great Lakes coastal wetlands in Lake Huron that had been drained for agriculture.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Changes in the abundance and diversity of coastal wetland fauna from the open water/macrophyte edge towards shore|doi=10.1023/A:1008447705647|year=1998|last1=Cardinale|first1=B.J.|last2=Brady|first2=V.J.|last3=Burton|first3=T.M.|journal=Wetlands Ecology and Management|volume=6|issue=1 |pages=59–68|bibcode=1998WetEM...6...59C |s2cid=7105065}}</ref> He showed that, once hydrologic connectivity is re-established, the vegetation of drained wetlands could be restored from existing seed banks that had survived nearly a hundred years of farming in agricultural soils. He also showed that certain forms of stocking and augmentation could help re-establish natural invertebrate communities that form the base of the wetland food webs.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Does Facilitation of Faunal Recruitment Benefit Ecosystem Restoration? An Experimental Study of Invertebrate Assemblages in Wetland Mesocosms|doi=10.1046/j.1526-100X.2002.01042.x|year=2002|last1=Brady|first1=Valerie J.|last2=Cardinale|first2=Bradley J.|last3=Gathman|first3=Joseph P.|last4=Burton|first4=Thomas M.|journal=Restoration Ecology|volume=10|issue=4|pages=617–626|bibcode=2002ResEc..10..617B |s2cid=14237251 }}</ref>

Later in his graduate studies, Cardinale turned attention towards [[stream restoration]] where he experimentally tested common techniques that are used to restore streams in the Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States. His work helped determine which techniques statistically enhance the recovery of biodiversity and important ecological processes, and which techniques have the highest success rates for restoration.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/251820688|title=The Influence of Substrate Heterogeneity on Biofilm Metabolism in a Stream Ecosystem}}</ref>

In the early 2010s, Cardinale worked on collaborative projects with biologists and geomorphologists to evaluate the success of gravel augmentation in restoring spawning habitat for endangered Chinook salmon. Working in a restored section of the Merced River in central California, he and his students demonstrated that gravel augmentation does, in fact, enhance spawning habitat for Chinook.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Juvenile Chinook salmon, Oncorhynchus tshawytscha, growth and diet in riverine habitat engineered to improve conditions for spawning|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2400.2012.00849.x|year=2012|last1=Utz|first1=R. M.|last2=Zeug|first2=S. C.|last3=Cardinale|first3=B. J.|journal=Fisheries Management and Ecology|volume=19|issue=5|pages=375–388|bibcode=2012FisME..19..375U }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=How Does Restored Habitat For Chinook Salmon (Oncorhynchus Tshawytscha) In The Merced River In California Compare With Other Chinook Stream?|year=2013 |doi=10.1002/rra.1604 |hdl=2027.42/97512 |s2cid=15441560|last1=Albertson |first1=L. K. |last2=Koenig |first2=L. E. |last3=Lewis |first3=B. L. |last4=Zeug |first4=S. C. |last5=Harrison |first5=L. R. |last6=Cardinale |first6=B. J. |journal=River Research and Applications |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=469–482 |bibcode=2013RivRA..29..469A |hdl-access=free }}</ref> But the practice also leads to abnormally mobile streambeds that can damage salmonid eggs, reduce the abundance and alter the composition of food items, and change feeding rates, survival and growth of native fish, including juvenile salmon that hatch from spawning beds.<ref>{{cite journal|title=How does coarse gravel augmentation affect early-stage Chinook salmon Oncorhynchus tshawytscha embryonic survivorship?|pmid = 23639149|year = 2013|last1 = Utz|first1 = R. M.|last2 = Mesick|first2 = C. F.|last3 = Cardinale|first3 = B. J.|last4 = Dunne|first4 = T.|journal = Journal of Fish Biology|volume = 82|issue = 5|pages = 1484–96|doi = 10.1111/jfb.12085| bibcode=2013JFBio..82.1484U |hdl = 2027.42/98336| s2cid=14835252 |hdl-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/240133403|title=Trophic ecology and population attributes of two resident non-game fishes in riverine habitat engineered to enhance salmon spawning success}}</ref>

In 2017, Cardinale established the Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research (CIGLR), which brings together academic institutions with government agencies and private businesses who work together on achieving sustainable use of the Great Lakes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mlive.com/news/ann-arbor/2017/05/federal_grant_helps_great_lake.html|title=University of Michigan has new Great Lakes research institute|date=22 May 2017 }}</ref> With funding from NOAA and the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, CIGLR and its 40+ scientific staff have worked on restoring Great Lakes Areas of Concern, restoration of coastal fish habitat, management of invasive species, and remediation of coastal zones impacted by harmful algal blooms and hypoxia.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ciglr.seas.umich.edu/|title=Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research}}</ref>

===Ecological design===
A final portion of Cardinale's research program lies at the intersection of ecology and engineering where he has used principles of ecological design to improve the efficiency and sustainability of human engineered ecosystems. He has completed a number of experiments and published several key papers showing that the composition of species in biological communities can be manipulated to maximize removal of pollutants from freshwater. In 2011, he published a paper in Nature showing that streams managed to maximize biodiversity of algae are more efficient at removing nutrient pollutants like nitrates from the water than less diverse systems.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/news/2011/110406/full/news.2011.216.html|title=Algae biodiversity cleans streams|year=2011 |doi=10.1038/news.2011.216 |last1=Gewin |first1=Virginia |journal=Nature |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Soon after, he extended this work to consider emerging contaminants, and showed that certain combinations of species could be manipulated to maximize removal of titanium-dioxide nanoparticles from stream water.<ref>{{cite journal|title=How do stream organisms respond to, and influence, the concentration of titanium dioxide nanoparticles? A mesocosm study with algae and herbivores|pmid = 22847763|year = 2012|last1 = Kulacki|first1 = K. J.|last2 = Cardinale|first2 = B. J.|last3 = Keller|first3 = A. A.|last4 = Bier|first4 = R.|last5 = Dickson|first5 = H.|journal = Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry|volume = 31|issue = 10|pages = 2414–22|doi = 10.1002/etc.1962| bibcode=2012EnvTC..31.2414K |hdl = 2027.42/93650| s2cid=9789074 |hdl-access = free}}</ref>

Cardinale has also examined how biological communities can be engineered to maximize erosion control, and minimize the loss of sediments from stream bottoms and riverbanks. He and his research group have shown that enhancing plant diversity of native vegetation along streambanks creates complex rooting systems that help reduce the chance of bank sloughing and failure.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Plant biodiversity effects in reducing fluvial erosion are limited to low species richness|pmid = 27008770|year = 2016|last1 = Allen|first1 = D. C.|last2 = Cardinale|first2 = B. J.|last3 = Wynn-Thompson|first3 = T.|journal = Ecology|volume = 97|issue = 1|pages = 17–24|doi = 10.1890/15-0800.1|doi-access = free| bibcode=2016Ecol...97...17A |hdl = 2027.42/117138|hdl-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323777418|title=Riparian plant biodiversity reduces stream channel migration rates in three rivers in Michigan, USA: Riparian plant biodiversity reduces stream channel migration rates}}</ref> In addition, they have shown that small insects that live on the bottom of streams can bind rocks together as they spin nets to construct their homes, and these nets significantly reduce the probability of streambed erosion during floods.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265053310|title=A mechanistic model linking insect (Hydropsychidae) silk nets to incipient sediment motion in gravel-bedded streams}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Aquatic macroinvertebrates stabilize gravel bed sediment: A test using silk net-spinning caddisflies in semi-natural river channels|pmc = 6314585|year = 2019|last1 = Albertson|first1 = L. K.|last2 = Sklar|first2 = L. S.|last3 = Cooper|first3 = S. D.|last4 = Cardinale|first4 = B. J.|journal = PLOS ONE|volume = 14|issue = 1|article-number = e0209087|pmid = 30601831|doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0209087|bibcode = 2019PLoSO..1409087A| doi-access=free }}</ref>

Since 2013, Cardinale has been studying how ecological design might be used to improve the efficiency and sustainability of algal biofuel systems.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://news.umich.edu/from-ponds-to-power-2m-to-perfect-algae-as-diesel-fuel/|title=From ponds to power: $2M to perfect algae as diesel fuel|date=2 October 2018 }}</ref> He and his lab group have shown that certain combinations of species can maximize the production of algal feedstocks, and that species combinations can be developed such that they are complimentary in their recycling of expensive fertilizers that are used to cultivate algae in outdoor ponds.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Ecological Stoichiometry Meets Ecological Engineering: Using Polycultures to Enhance the Multifunctionality of Algal Biocrude Systems|doi=10.1021/acs.est.7b02137|pmid=28825799|year=2017|last1=Godwin|first1=Casey M.|last2=Hietala|first2=David C.|last3=Lashaway|first3=Aubrey R.|last4=Narwani|first4=Anita|last5=Savage|first5=Phillip E.|last6=Cardinale|first6=Bradley J.|journal=Environmental Science & Technology|volume=51|issue=19|pages=11450–11458|bibcode=2017EnST...5111450G|url=https://www.dora.lib4ri.ch/eawag/islandora/object/eawag%3A15360 }}</ref> Further, he has shown that nesting complimentary species within more diverse communities of algae can help alleviate problems associated with pathogens, parasites, and predators that often cause feedstocks to crash.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325820311|title=Biodiversity improves the ecological design of sustainable biofuel systems}}</ref>
